PODCAST FEED VALIDATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Will Apple Podcasts accept your feed?

Paste your podcast's RSS feed XML and check it against the documented Apple Podcasts feed requirements and the RSS 2.0 spec: missing channel title, description, language, category, explicit rating, or artwork; a per-episode enclosure, pubDate, or title problem; a pubDate not in RFC 822 format; and duplicate episode guids — the documented cause of an episode silently reappearing as new or disappearing from a podcast app.

Nothing is uploaded. The feed XML you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device — see "Why can't this page fetch my feed URL itself?" below for what the CLI adds.

1. Check a feed

Get this by opening your feed URL in a browser tab and using "View Page Source" or "Save As", or with curl -s <your-feed-url>.

2. Results

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

The CLI fetches your feed URL for real, over HTTP — no cross-origin restriction, because it isn't a browser:

node check.mjs https://example.com/feed.xml --json
node check.mjs https://example.com/feed.xml --timeout 20000

Get check.mjs, fetch-feed.mjs, feed-parser.mjs, and engine.mjs from the repo — plain Node 18+, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the feed URL you give it — nothing goes through this site. Exit code 1 when a danger-severity finding is produced or the feed could not be fetched.

What's checked

CheckWhat it flagsSeverity
Missing channel title / description / language / linkRSS 2.0 spec and Apple Podcasts required elementsDanger
Missing or unrecognized itunes:categoryRequired for Apple Podcasts submission; checked against Apple's documented top-level listDanger / Notice
Missing or invalid itunes:explicitMust be the current boolean true/false formatDanger / Notice
Missing itunes:image, or wrong file extensionCover artwork required for submissionDanger / Notice
Missing atom:link rel=selfFeed-portability best practiceNotice
Episode missing title / enclosure / pubDateRequired per-episode elementsDanger
pubDate not in RFC 822 formatThe RSS 2.0 spec's required date formatDanger
Duplicate item guidDocumented cause of an episode disappearing or reappearing as newDanger
guid marked as a permalink but not a URLisPermaLink defaults to true; a non-URL value should set it falseNotice

More: why podcast feeds fail validation, and the two bugs that cost the most. See also: how this differs from the W3C Feed Validator.

Common questions

Why does Apple Podcasts reject or silently ignore my episode?

Almost always a specific, documented feed-spec violation: a missing required element (itunes:category, itunes:explicit, cover artwork), an item missing its enclosure or pubDate, or a pubDate that is not in the RFC 822 format the RSS 2.0 spec requires. Apple Podcasts' own feed processor is strict about these — this tool checks your feed against the same documented rules before you submit or re-submit.

Why did an old episode reappear as new, or disappear entirely?

The most common documented cause is a duplicate <guid> value across two items. Podcast apps use guid to decide whether an item is one they have already shown a subscriber — if a feed generator reuses a guid (or falls back to an unstable one), an app can treat a later item as an update to an earlier one, making it vanish, or resurface an old episode as unseen.

Why can't this page fetch my feed URL itself?

A browser page's fetch() to a different origin is blocked by CORS unless that server explicitly opts in with an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header — most podcast hosts do not set this for arbitrary third-party pages, since a feed being reachable does not mean its owner meant for any website to read it client-side. Rather than fail silently for feeds that do not opt in, this page always works from pasted XML. The zero-dependency CLI has no such restriction because it isn't a browser tab — it makes one real HTTP request directly to the feed URL.

Is this a full Apple Podcasts submission checklist?

No. It checks specific, mechanically verifiable properties of the feed XML you provide — required elements, format validity, and duplicate/unstable guids. It is not a guarantee Apple, Spotify, or any other podcast app will accept or display your show, and it does not check account-level submission steps.

It reports whether the feed XML you provided satisfies specific, mechanically checkable rules — nothing more. It is not a guarantee that Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or any other podcast app will accept or display your show. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything you paste runs in your browser and is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over the same show: YouTube Chapters Checker converts episode markers into a podcast chapters.json. Social Preview Checker checks how a link to your show's site renders when shared. hreflang Reciprocity Checker checks a multi-language site's own language-link tags. Sitemap lastmod Freshness Check checks whether a sitemap's freshness dates hold up.

vs-w3c-feed-validator.html.text:
← Podcast Feed Validator

Podcast Feed Validator vs. the W3C Feed Validator

The W3C Feed Validator is a long-established, free, generic tool: point it at a feed URL and it checks the XML is well-formed and conforms to the general RSS or Atom syndication-format specifications. Based on its own public description, it is a solid, established first stop for "is this even valid XML in a syndication format" — the same job for RSS/Atom feeds that a markup validator does for HTML.

Podcast Feed Validator does a narrower, podcast-specific job. The iTunes and Podcast namespace elements Apple Podcasts actually requires — itunes:category, itunes:explicit, itunes:image, per-episode itunes:episodeType — are a separate namespace layered on top of general RSS, defined after and outside the base spec a general validator checks against. A feed can be perfectly well-formed, spec-conformant RSS and still be missing every element Apple's Podcasts Connect requires for submission. This tool checks those elements specifically, plus two podcast-app-specific failure modes a general validator has no reason to look for: a pubDate not in the RFC 822 format podcast apps expect, and a duplicate guid across episodes — the documented cause of an episode disappearing or reappearing as new in a subscriber's app.

QuestionWhere to answer it
My feed URL won't parse at all, or I'm not sure it's well-formed XML. W3C Feed Validator — general well-formedness is its job.
My feed is valid RSS but Apple Podcasts rejected the submission, or an episode isn't showing up. Podcast Feed Validator — checks the iTunes/Podcast-namespace elements a general validator doesn't know about.
An old episode reappeared as new, or a recent one vanished. Podcast Feed Validator's duplicate-guid check — a general RSS validator has no reason to flag two valid, well-formed items sharing a guid value.
I want this checked automatically on every publish, with nothing sent to a third party. Podcast Feed Validator's CLI — node check.mjs <feed-url> runs from your own machine and exits non-zero on a finding, wireable into any CI or publish script as an ordinary step.

Neither tool replaces the other. Run the W3C Feed Validator first if you're not sure the XML itself is sound; run this one for the podcast-specific requirements that actually decide whether Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other podcast apps accept and correctly display your show.

Common questions

Should I use Podcast Feed Validator or the W3C Feed Validator?

Different jobs, and many podcasters need both at different times. The W3C Feed Validator, based on its own public description, checks that a feed is well-formed, spec-conformant XML against the general RSS/Atom syndication formats — it is the right first stop for a feed that won't parse at all. Podcast Feed Validator instead checks the iTunes/Podcast-namespace elements and podcast-app-specific rules the W3C tool has no knowledge of: itunes:category against Apple's own taxonomy, itunes:explicit's current boolean format, cover artwork, and the guid/pubDate bugs that cause an episode to disappear or reappear in a subscriber's app.

Does the W3C Feed Validator check Apple Podcasts' requirements?

Based on its own public description, no — it validates against the general RSS 2.0 and Atom syndication-format specifications, which predate and do not include the iTunes/Podcast namespace Apple defines separately for podcast-specific metadata (category, explicit rating, episode type, artwork). A feed can pass general RSS well-formedness and still be missing every element Apple's Podcasts Connect actually requires.

Is this page affiliated with the W3C?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) or its Feed Validator. It is named here only to describe what that tool does and how it differs from this one, based on its own public description.

More: why podcast feeds fail validation.

why-podcast-feeds-fail-validation.html.text:
← Podcast Feed Validator

Why podcast feeds fail validation

A podcast RSS feed is just XML, and almost any well-formed-enough XML renders fine in a browser or a lenient reader. Apple Podcasts' own feed processor, and most podcast apps' parsers, are stricter than that — and the gap between "displays fine" and "satisfies the documented spec" is where a show's episodes quietly stop showing up.

The two bugs that cost the most

Most validation failures are a missing required element — annoying, but the fix is obvious the moment you see the finding. Two failure modes are worse, because the feed looks fine and the failure shows up somewhere else entirely, later, as a confused subscriber.

A duplicate <guid>

Podcast apps use an episode's guid, not its title or its position in the feed, to decide whether it is one a subscriber has already been shown. If a feed generator produces the same guid for two different items — often because the guid is derived from something that turns out not to be unique, like an episode number that got reused after a renumbering — one of two things happens: the second item gets treated as a silent edit to the first and never appears as new, or an app's local cache gets confused enough to resurface an old episode as unread. Neither shows up by looking at the feed; both show up as "why did episode 40 disappear?" in a support inbox.

A <pubDate> that isn't RFC 822

The RSS 2.0 spec requires pubDate in RFC 822 date-time format — something like Wed, 02 Oct 2024 15:00:00 GMT. A format that a human (and many lenient parsers) can read perfectly well, like an ISO 8601 date (2024-10-02) or a locale-formatted string, is not valid RSS even though it looks like a date. A strict parser is entitled to reject it outright, sort the episode into the wrong place in the timeline, or drop it from the feed altogether — and because the date still looks like a date to anyone reading the XML by eye, this is one of the easiest mistakes to ship without noticing.

The missing-element failures, briefly

Apple's documented requirements are exacting at the channel level: a title, a description (or itunes:summary), a language code, at least one itunes:category from Apple's own taxonomy, an itunes:explicit value in the current boolean true/false format, and cover artwork declared via itunes:image. Any one of these missing blocks a submission outright — see the checker on the main page for the complete list, including the per-episode requirements (title, enclosure, pubDate).

A feed that renders is not a feed that validates

The most common way any of this goes unnoticed is testing by opening the feed URL in a browser and seeing that it displays. A browser's XML rendering is far more forgiving than Apple's ingestion pipeline or a strict podcast app's parser — "it looks fine" and "it satisfies the documented spec" are different claims, and the second one is what actually determines whether an episode reaches a subscriber.

Check your own feed: Podcast Feed Validator. See also: how this differs from the W3C Feed Validator.

Common questions

What is the single most common reason a podcast feed fails Apple's review?

A missing required element — most often itunes:category, itunes:explicit, or the cover-artwork itunes:image tag. Apple's feed processor requires these at the channel level for every show; a feed missing any one of them cannot be submitted at all, regardless of how good the episodes are.

What is the guid bug, and why is it the expensive one?

Two <item> elements sharing the same <guid> value. Podcast apps use guid, not the episode's title or position in the feed, to decide whether an item is one a subscriber has already been shown. A generator that reuses a guid — often because it derives the guid from something that isn't actually unique, like an episode number that got reused after a renumbering — causes one of two failures: the second item is treated as an edit to the first and never shown as new, or (worse) the change confuses an app's local cache into re-showing an old episode as unread. Both bugs are invisible in the feed's own rendered output and only show up as a support ticket from a confused subscriber.

Why does the pubDate format matter so much?

The RSS 2.0 spec requires pubDate in RFC 822 date-time format (e.g. "Wed, 02 Oct 2024 15:00:00 GMT"). A different but still human-readable format — an ISO 8601 date like "2024-10-02", or a locale-formatted string — is technically invalid RSS even though most humans and many lenient parsers can read it. A strict podcast-app parser is entitled to reject the date, sort the episode incorrectly, or drop it from the feed's timeline entirely, and this is a documented, recurring cause of an episode appearing in the wrong order or not appearing at all.

Does a feed that renders fine in a browser mean it's valid?

No. A browser (or a lenient RSS reader) tolerates almost any well-formed-enough XML and will happily display a feed that Apple's stricter, spec-conformant processor rejects outright. "It looks fine when I open the URL" and "it satisfies the documented spec" are different claims, and the gap between them is exactly what a feed validator checks.
